lesson.title: 444 Days: The Iranian Hostage Crisis
lesson.summary: When Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy in Tehran in November 1979 and took American diplomats hostage, the crisis dragged on for 444 days and came to symbolize the limits of American power in the final year of Jimmy Carter's presidency.
lesson.body:
The roots of the crisis lay in Iran's 1978 to 1979 revolution, which overthrew Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the Shah of Iran, a longtime American ally whose government had grown deeply unpopular for its repression and its close ties to the United States. In February 1979, the exiled Shiite cleric Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned to Iran and helped establish an Islamic Republic, and anti American sentiment ran high among revolutionaries who associated the United States with the Shah's rule, including a CIA backed coup in Iran back in 1953 that had helped keep the Shah in power for decades.

Tensions boiled over after President Carter allowed the exiled Shah to enter the United States in October 1979 for cancer treatment. On November 4, 1979, a group of Iranian students, with the later backing of the revolutionary government, stormed the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and took its staff hostage, demanding that the United States return the Shah to Iran to stand trial. Most of the hostages taken that day, fifty two Americans, were held for the rest of the crisis, which stretched on for 444 days.

The crisis dominated American political life through 1980. Carter pursued diplomatic pressure and economic sanctions against Iran, and in April 1980 he authorized a military rescue mission, Operation Eagle Claw, which ended in disaster when helicopters malfunctioned in a desert staging area and a collision during the withdrawal killed eight American servicemen, and the mission was aborted before reaching Tehran. The failed rescue humiliated the administration and reinforced a public sense that the country was powerless to protect its own citizens abroad, an impression that badly damaged Carter's already struggling reelection campaign against Ronald Reagan in 1980.

The hostages were finally released on January 20, 1981, just minutes after Reagan was sworn in as president, the result of last minute negotiations, mediated by Algeria, in which the United States agreed to unfreeze billions of dollars in Iranian assets. The timing meant Carter never got the political credit for the resolution he had worked toward for over a year. The crisis left a lasting mark on American politics and on U.S. relations with Iran, and it became one of the defining reasons voters turned toward Reagan's promise of restored American strength, connecting directly to the Reagan Revolution that began that same day.
